fetched_contents.text: The Effects of Cannabinoids on Pro- and Anti-Inflammatory Cytokines: A Systematic Review of In Vivo Studies Abstract Introduction: Some cannabinoids have been identified as anti-inflammatory agents; however, their potential therapeutic or prophylactic applications remain controversial. The aim of this systematic review was to provide a timely and comprehensive insight into cannabinoid-mediated pro- and anti-inflammatory cytokine responses in preclinical in vivo studies. Methods and Materials: A systematic search was conducted using PubMed, Web of Science, EMBASE, and Scopus. Eligible studies where cannabinoids had been evaluated for their effect on inflammation in animal models were included in the analysis. Data were extracted from 26 of 4247 eligible full text articles, and risk of bias was assessed using the SYstematic Review Center for Laboratory animal Experimentation (SYRCLE) tool. Studies examined cannabidiol (CBD; n=20); cannabigerol (CBG; n=1); delta 9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC; n=2); THC and CBD separately (n=1); and THC and CBD in combination (n=2). Results: Tumor necrosis factor alpha, interleukin (IL)-1β, IL-6, and interferon gamma were the most commonly studied pro-inflammatory cytokines and their levels were consistently reduced after treatment with CBD, CBG, or CBD+THC, but not with THC alone. The association between cannabinoid-induced anti-inflammatory response and disease severity was examined. In 22 studies where CBD, CBG, or CBD in combination with THC were administered, a reduction in the levels of at least one inflammatory cytokine was observed, and in 24 studies, some improvements in disease or disability were apparent. THC alone did not reduce pro-inflammatory cytokine levels (n=3), but resulted in improvements in neuropathic pain in one study. Conclusions: This review shows that CBD, CBG, and CBD+THC combination exert a predominantly anti-inflammatory effect in vivo, whereas THC alone does not reduce pro-inflammatory or increase anti-inflammatory cytokines. It is anticipated that this information could be used to inform human clinical trials of cannabinoids, focusing on CBD and CBG to reduce inflammation across a range of pathophysiological processes. Keywords: anti-inflammatory, cannabinoids, cannabis, CBD, cytokines, inflammation, systematic review, THC Introduction Cannabis sativa is a complex botanical containing ∼500 phytochemicals of which 60 or more belong to the phytocannabinoid class. These phytochemical compounds have been used for >6000 years to treat diseases.1 Cannabinoid compounds act on the endocannabinoid system (ECS) that consists of cannabinoid type 1 (CB1) and type 2 (CB2) receptors, their endogenous ligands (endocannabinoids), and the enzymes responsible for their synthesis and degradation.2 Primarily, CB2 receptors, and to a lesser extent CB1 receptors, are involved in regulating the immune response, diminishing inflammatory responses by inhibiting the release of pro-inflammatory mediators and through immune cell modulation.2 Cannabinoids also modulate several noncannabinoid receptors and ion channels and act through various receptor-independent pathways—for example, by delaying the reuptake of endocannabinoids and neurotransmitters (such as anandamide and adenosine) and by enhancing or inhibiting the binding action of certain G-protein-coupled receptors.2,3 Reported therapeutic benefits of exogenous cannabinoids (plant derived and synthetic) on the ECS include analgesic, anti-inflammatory, anti-emetic, and anticonvulsive effects as well as improved muscle tone, mood state, cognition, and appetite.3–8 The ECS is therefore an emerging target to treat a wide range of pathological conditions, particularly those related to inflammation.9 Inflammation is a complex sequence of events that occurs in response to harmful stimuli, and is a vital part of the immune response to damage caused by trauma, infection, or environmental factors. Whereas the inflammatory response is essential and beneficial to a host in the short term, excessive or persistent inflammation can cause pain, tissue damage, and is associated with many chronic conditions such as diabetes, dementia, multiple sclerosis (MS), and rheumatoid arthritis.10 Cytokines are potent soluble immune mediators that are modulated in various disease states.11 Pro-inflammatory responses are characterized by increased levels of cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α), interleukin (IL)-6, IL-1β, and interferon gamma (IFN-γ), and these drive the progression of chronic disease.12 Conversely, anti-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-10 mediate the opposing effect.12 Chronic inflammatory conditions can be prevented and better managed by regulating or inhibiting excessive or persistent inflammation through anti-inflammatory compounds that act on the ECS, such as exogenous cannabinoids.13 In recent times, regulations that previously restricted scientific study of cannabis and its constituents have become more relaxed internationally. As a result, interest in the therapeutic potential of cannabis has increased.14 Despite this recent research intensity, systematic reviews undertaken to critically appraise human trials of medicinal cannabis have, in general, found only modest benefit to patients15–18; yet, many cannabis users report great benefit for conditions for which compelling evidence is lacking.19 It is timely to critically evaluate the preclinical in vivo evidence so that interventions can be appropriately targeted in subsequent human trials. Therefore, in this review, we focus on the animal models of inflammation that researchers have used to investigate the therapeutic effects of cannabinoids. We aimed to systematically summarize and review studies that evaluate the in vivo effect of cannabinoids on pro- and anti-inflammatory cytokines. fetched_contents.text: Cannabis and Rheumatoid Arthritis: A Scoping Review Evaluating the Benefits, Risks, and Future Research Directions Abstract Rheumatoid diseases, including rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, and fibromyalgia, are characterized by progressive inflammation in the musculoskeletal system, predominantly affecting the joints and leading to cartilage and bone damage. The resulting pain and ongoing degradation of the musculoskeletal system contribute to reduced physical activity, ultimately impacting quality of life and imposing a substantial socioeconomic burden. Unfortunately, current therapeutics have limited efficacy in slowing disease progression and managing pain. Thus, the development of novel and alternative therapies is imperative. Cannabinoids possess beneficial properties as potential treatments for rheumatoid diseases due to their anti-inflammatory and analgesic properties. Preclinical studies have demonstrated promising results in halting disease progression and relieving pain. However, there is a scarcity of patient clinical studies, and the available data show mixed results. Consequently, there are currently no established clinical recommendations regarding the utilization of cannabis for treating rheumatoid diseases. In this review, we aim to explore the concept of cannabis use for rheumatoid diseases, including potential adverse effects. We will provide an overview of the data obtained from preclinical and clinical trials and from retrospective studies on the efficacy and safety of cannabis in the treatment of rheumatoid diseases. Keywords: Autoimmune disease, cannabis, CBD, inflammation, rheumatoid arthritis, THC INTRODUCTION Rheumatoid diseases are characterized by progressive chronic inflammation of the musculoskeletal system, afflicting primarily the joints but can lead to systemic comorbidities, such as pulmonary diseases or vasculitis. Chronic inflammation results in cartilage and bone damage, whose deterioration can lead to the disability of the affected patient.1 Rheumatoid diseases inflict a significant individual and societal burden. Pain and musculoskeletal deficits lead to a progressive decline in physical activity and quality of life and carry the risk of cumulative comorbidities.2 In addition, medical costs for treatment, as well as reduced work capacity and decreased societal participation of patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA), have a significant socioeconomic effect on society.3 Treating rheumatoid disease is challenging not only because of its progressive nature but also because of the side effects of available therapies.4 Moreover, available treatment options cannot reverse rheumatoid diseases. Thus, therapy efforts are divided into preventive medicine (starting treatment before clinical manifestation) and developing new drugs. Three classes of drugs are currently available: (1) disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs), which target tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-α, the interleukin (IL)-6 receptor, and stimulate the depletion of T and B cells, thereby slowing the progression of the structural damage;5,6 (2) non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, which improve physical function by reducing pain and stiffness, but do not modify disease progression;4 and (3) glucocorticosteroids, which have a rapid symptomatic and disease-modifying effect.7 Prolonged use of glucocorticoids and DMARDs has long-term severe adverse effects.8,9 Moreover, patients treated with biological DMARDs have an increased risk of severe infections by tuberculosis and herpes zoster virus, as well as an elevated risk of developing melanoma.10 This exemplifies the need for novel treatment approaches and safe therapeutics. One approach is medicinal cannabis use, which takes advantage of its pain-reducing and immune-modulating features. CANNABIS AND CANNABINOIDS Cannabis is the most widely used illicit drug in the world. Cannabis is not a single substance but consists of more than 550 different chemical constituents accumulated in the cannabis plant, among them approximately 150 psychoactive and non-psychoactive cannabinoids and over 400 non-cannabinoids. The cannabis plant (Cannabis sativa) belongs to the Cannabaceae family. There are two major forms of Cannabis sativa: marijuana, which has high levels of the psychoactive tetrahydrocannabinol (THC); and hemp, which has high levels of non-psychoactive cannabinoids and low THC levels.11 The two main pharmacologically active THC compounds are Δ8-THC and Δ9-THC. The main non-psychoactive pharmacologically active cannabinoids include cannabinol, cannabidiol (CBD), and cannabigerol (Figure 1), as well as non-cannabinoids like flavonoids, terpenes, and fatty acids.12,13 Cannabinoids mediate their biological and therapeutic effects through the G-protein coupled receptors cannabinoid receptor 1 (CB1R) and 2 (CB2R).14–16 The G-proteins act as adaptors that link G-protein coupled receptors to intracellular signaling and regulatory proteins to activate or modulate signaling pathways. Other G-protein coupled receptors, such as GPR55 and GPR18, and transient receptor potential (TRP) channels, such as TRPV2, TRPA1, and TRPM8, are also involved in cannabinoid signaling.17 Highly expressed in the central nervous system, CB1R is found in particularly high levels in the neocortex, hippocampus, basal ganglia, cerebellum, and brainstem.18 Conversely, low expression levels are observed in the peripheral nervous system. The CB1R binds the main active ingredient of marijuana, Δ9-THC, and mediates most of the THC effects in the central nervous system.19 The CB2R is present at high levels in the immune system and is commonly associated with regulating immune function. Additionally, CB2R is also located in the brain,20 where it is primarily localized to microglia, the central nervous system resident macrophages.21 The fact that both CB1 and CB2 receptors are expressed by immune cells suggests that cannabinoids play an important role in immune system regulation. Submission received: 18 July 2024 / Revised: 26 August 2024 / Accepted: 27 August 2024 / Published: 29 August 2024 Abstract The management of rheumatic diseases has noticeably changed in recent years with the development of targeted therapeutic agents, namely, biological disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs. Identifying essential signaling pathways and factors crucial for the development and progression of these diseases remains a significant challenge. Therapy could be used to delay the onset or reduce harm. The endocannabinoid system’s presence within the synovium can be identified as a suggested target for therapeutic interventions due to its role in modulating pain, inflammation, and joint metabolism. This review brings together the most pertinent information concerning the actions of the endocannabinoid system present in inflamed synovial tissue and its interaction with phytocannabinoids and synthetic cannabinoids, which can be used from a therapeutic perspective to minimize the inflammatory and pain processes typical of osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis. 1. Introduction Rheumatic diseases, notably, osteoarthritis (OA) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) represent a public health issue, and the costs of prevention by reducing the risk factors or treating patients are much lower than those generated by hospitalization and surgeries [1]. Several treatments for OA and RA can alleviate disease symptoms and slow their progression. The ideal approach requires an early diagnosis, proper pharmacological treatments and non-pharmacological treatments such as exercise and physical therapy. Adequate therapy aims to obtain remission and reduce side effects [2]. However, an incomplete understanding of both diseases’ etiology makes it challenging to discover a curative treatment [3]. Considering that the significant pathological changes occurring in both OA and RA include damage to articular cartilage, subchondral bone, synovium, and articular capsule, these tissues have been identified as potential targets for pharmacological therapies. In particular, the endocannabinoid system (ECS) in the synovium could serve as a therapeutic target due to its role in controlling pain, inflammation, and joint metabolism. Phytocannabinoids and synthetic cannabinoids can interact with ECS components, amplifying their anti-inflammatory and analgesic effects or inhibiting pro-inflammatory and pain pathways [4]. Furthermore, cannabinoids can improve the well-being of patients by enhancing sleep, appetite, and mood [5]. However, there are still gaps regarding efficacy, the dose-dependent curve, tolerability, drug interaction, expected adverse effects, and safety [6]. Up to now, the clinical use of cannabinoids has been reported only in a few studies with small sample sizes and for short periods [7]. Only a limited number of products have been approved for therapy, and the legislation and classification process are still non-uniform and inadequate. Due to the lack of evidence-based data on safety profiles, clinicians struggle to make decisions about tailoring optimal therapy for each patient suffering from rheumatic disease [8], fearing ethical and legal issues [9]. Patients often resort to self-medication using certain products to relieve pain. It is worth noting that subjective opinions can have an impact on the reported results. Additionally, there can be issues associated with respiratory adverse effects and psychological implications, such as addiction to self-medication. Conversely, prejudice against those compounds also makes the situation complicated [8,9]. This review presents the most relevant data on the activity of endocannabinoids present in inflamed synovial tissue and their interaction with phytocannabinoids and synthetic cannabinoids from a therapeutic perspective, aiming to reduce the inflammation and pain processes typical of OA and RA. 2. Search Strategy and Manuscript Selection We performed a comprehensive search according to the review strategies recommended by Gasparyan et al. [10]. We conducted the search through the PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science databases, using the keywords “cannabinoids”, “endocannbinoids”, phytocannabinoids”, synthetic cannabinoids”, “osteoarthritis”, rheumatoid arthritis”, “rheumatic diseases”, and “synovium”. We reviewed 115 articles and included 65. Non-English sources, conference abstracts, and non-peer-reviewed sources were not included. 3. Rheumatic Diseases 3.1. Osteoarthritis OA has been considered a disease resulting from gradual deterioration and damage (“wear and tear”), mainly impacting bone and cartilage. Recent advancements have revealed it to be a complex disorder involving the whole synovial joint [11]. Articular cartilage deterioration, subchondral bone thickening, osteophyte development, synovium inflammation, ligament damage, and capsule hypertrophy are the pathologic features of OA [12]. The etiology is multifactorial, involving genetic, constitutional, and environmental components. The widely accepted hypothesis of OA pathogenesis implicates an initial injury, frequently biomechanical, which leads to the release of mediators that activate different inflammatory pathways [13]. Evidence for pain reduction and analgesic mechanisms

Cannabinoids show consistent evidence of reducing both mechanical and inflammatory pain in animal models of arthritis, with the available evidence emphasizing anti-inflammatory contributions rather than purely central analgesia. A review on cannabinoids and pain states that cannabinoids may contribute to pain relief through an anti-inflammatory action [N3-R1], and another review notes that analgesic effects are supported by interactions between TRPV1 and CB1 in inflamed tissue [N3-R2]. A broader review on cannabinoids in chronic pain reports that interventions targeting CB1 or CB2 receptors improve pain outcomes in a variety of preclinical pain models [N3-R3], which is directly relevant to arthritis-related pain relief.

The role of endocannabinoid receptors in pain relief is best understood as receptor-dependent and overlapping. TRPV1 is highlighted as mediating inflammatory pain, and TRPV1/CB1 co-expression is enhanced in inflamed tissue [N3-R2]. CB1 and CB2 receptors are both pharmacologically active in arthritis-related settings: CB1 is highly expressed in the central nervous system and mediates many THC effects, while CB2 is present at high levels in the immune system and is involved in immune regulation [N2-F1]. This receptor context matters because it implies that cannabinoids can act both centrally and peripherally, with CB1 more likely to mediate central analgesia and CB2 more likely to mediate immune and peripheral anti-inflammatory effects [N2-F1]. The evidence base in the provided materials does not clearly separate “central vs peripheral analgesia” into mutually exclusive categories, but it does support the idea that cannabinoids modulate pain through both receptor systems and through inflammatory suppression [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3].

Evidence for central versus peripheral analgesia is thinner in the provided search results than for general pain relief. The strongest direct statement is that TRPV1 mediates inflammatory pain and that TRPV1/CB1 co-expression is increased in inflamed tissue, suggesting that some analgesic effects may involve both TRPV1 and CB1 [N3-R2]. The broader cannabinoid review also notes that the endocannabinoid system is involved in tissue healing under inflammatory conditions [N3-R4], which implies that pain relief can arise from anti-inflammatory and repair processes rather than only from direct sensory inhibition. The animal arthritis literature referenced here is less explicit on central vs peripheral mechanisms than on overall pain reduction [N2-F1], so the conclusion should be cautious: cannabinoids reduce pain, and the mechanism appears to be multimodal, with CB1 and CB2 contributing in different ways, and TRPV1 playing a key role in inflammatory pain [N3-R2][N3-R3][N2-F1].

Overall, the evidence supports that cannabinoids reduce mechanical and inflammatory pain in arthritis models, with analgesia linked to CB1, CB2, and TRPV1, and with some indication of both central and peripheral contributions [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3]. However, the provided evidence is less detailed on a strict separation of central vs peripheral analgesia than on the broader anti-inflammatory and receptor-based pain mechanism [N3-R4].

Biological pathways linking cannabinoids to anti-inflammatory effects in arthritis

The provided evidence shows that cannabinoids primarily act through CB1 and CB2 receptors, with CB2 being especially central to immune and inflammatory regulation. A systematic review of in vivo studies reports that cannabinoids act on inflammation through mechanisms different from NSAIDs, and that CBD, CBG, and CBD+THC exert a predominantly anti-inflammatory effect in vivo, whereas THC alone does not reduce pro-inflammatory cytokines [N1-F2]. This is a strong starting point for understanding the anti-inflammatory pathway.

Cannabinoid signaling also extends beyond classical receptors. The same review notes that cannabinoids modulate several non-cannabinoid receptors and ion channels, and act through receptor-independent pathways, including delaying reuptake of endocannabinoids and neurotransmitters, and enhancing or inhibiting G-protein-coupled receptor binding [N1-F2]. This broadens the mechanism beyond receptor occupancy and suggests that anti-inflammatory effects can arise from multiple signaling layers. The search result on the CB2 receptor further emphasizes that CB2 mediates inflammation in vitro, in animal models, and in the context of clinical trials [N1-R5], reinforcing that CB2 is a key anti-inflammatory target.

How cannabinoids suppress cytokine production and immune activation is supported by direct cytokine evidence. The systematic review found that TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, and IFN-γ were most commonly studied pro-inflammatory cytokines, and that CBD, CBG, or CBD+THC reduced their levels in vivo, whereas THC alone did not [N1-F2]. In other words, cannabinoids suppress cytokine-driven immune activation by lowering key pro-inflammatory mediators, rather than simply suppressing pain or behavior. The review also notes that the association between cannabinoid-induced anti-inflammatory response and disease severity was examined, and that improvements in disease or disability were apparent in many studies [N1-F2]. This supports the idea that anti-inflammatory effects translate into reduced immune activation and disease burden.

Evidence for anti-fibrotic or anti-angiogenic effects in joint tissue is more limited in the provided material, but still present. The synovium-focused MDPI review states that the endocannabinoid system is present in the inflamed synovium and can be a target for rheumatic diseases, with implications for pain, inflammation, and joint metabolism [N4-F3]. It also notes that cannabinoids can be used from a therapeutic perspective to minimize inflammatory and pain processes typical of OA and RA [N4-F3]. While this does not directly state anti-fibrotic or anti-angiogenic effects, it does support the broader idea that cannabinoids can act on joint tissue biology beyond cytokines, and that synovial inflammation is a key target [N4-F3]. The synovium review also mentions that inflamed synovial tissue is the site where endocannabinoids interact with phytocannabinoids and synthetic cannabinoids [N4-F3], which is relevant to localized joint effects.

The evidence from the synovium review also indirectly supports anti-fibrotic-like effects by describing articular cartilage damage, synovium inflammation, and subchondral bone changes as major pathological features of arthritis [N4-F3]. The review’s focus on the endocannabinoid system’s role in controlling pain, inflammation, and joint metabolism implies that cannabinoids may reduce tissue-destructive processes associated with fibrosis or repair failure [N4-F3]. However, the provided evidence does not give direct statements on anti-fibrotic or anti-angiogenic effects in joint tissue; those conclusions should therefore be treated as plausible mechanistic extensions rather than directly supported claims [N4-F3].

Overall, the evidence points to a clear anti-inflammatory pathway through CB1 and CB2 receptors, cytokine suppression, immune modulation, and broader joint tissue regulation via the endocannabinoid system [N1-F2][N1-R5][N4-F3]. Anti-fibrotic or anti-angiogenic effects are not explicitly confirmed in the provided search results, but the synovium literature supports the idea that cannabinoids can act on inflammatory and structural joint biology [N4-F3].

Evidence from chronic inflammatory arthritis animal models

The animal-model evidence in the provided search results is centered on collagen-induced arthritis (CIA) and related joint disease models. A scoping review on cannabis and rheumatoid arthritis reports that oral or intraperitoneal CBD has an anti-arthritic effect in acute and chronic relapsing CIA [N2-R1]. Another search result states that the goal of a study was to determine the antiarthritic potential of delta-8-tetrahydrocannabinol (Δ8-THC) using the collagen-induced arthritis model in rats [N2-R3]. A separate search result mentions that CBD is an oral anti-arthritic therapeutic in murine CIA [N6-R3], while another notes that the scoping review includes clinical and preclinical data on rheumatoid diseases [N2-F1]. This establishes CIA as the dominant model in the provided evidence, with some attention to broader rheumatic-disease context.

Outcome measures assessed in these studies are largely inflammatory and structural. The scoping review highlights that preclinical studies have demonstrated promising results in halting disease progression and relieving pain [N2-F1]. The evidence also indicates that the main outcome-related endpoints include disease progression, pain relief, and possibly clinical signs of inflammation, although the exact measures are not all explicitly listed in the excerpts. The review on the endocannabinoid system in inflamed synovium states that cannabinoids can be used from a therapeutic perspective to minimize inflammatory and pain processes typical of OA and RA [N4-F3], which implies that outcome measures often include inflammation, synovial changes, and pain. The synovium review also notes that the endocannabinoid system is present in the inflamed synovium and that phytocannabinoids and synthetic cannabinoids can interact with ECS components to amplify anti-inflammatory and analgesic effects [N4-F3], supporting the use of synovial inflammation and joint metabolism as outcome domains.

The scoping review states that CBD has an anti-arthritic effect in CIA and that preclinical studies have demonstrated promising results in halting disease progression and relieving pain [N2-R1][N2-F1]. The synovium review adds that the endocannabinoid system can be used to minimize inflammatory and pain processes typical of RA and OA, and that the synovium is a site of joint inflammation and tissue changes [N4-F3]. However, the evidence does not uniformly state that all studies reduced cartilage damage or bone erosion; rather, it indicates that cannabinoids can reduce inflammation, pain, and disease progression [N2-R1][N2-F1][N4-F3]. The provided search excerpts do not give a direct, single consensus that every study improved all three endpoints, so the safest conclusion is that cannabinoids have been shown to reduce joint inflammation and pain, with promising evidence for halting disease progression, but less explicit uniformity on cartilage and bone outcomes across the cited studies [N2-R1][N2-F1][N4-F3].

Dose-response and time-course patterns are only partially visible in the excerpts. The scoping review notes that CBD has an anti-arthritic effect in both oral and intraperitoneal administration in acute and chronic relapsing CIA [N2-R1], suggesting that route and delivery method can affect outcomes. The review also states that preclinical studies have demonstrated promising results in halting disease progression and relieving pain, but it does not provide a detailed dose-response curve [N2-F1]. The same scoping review mentions that CBD, CBG, and CBD+THC exert a predominantly anti-inflammatory effect in vivo, while THC alone does not reduce pro-inflammatory cytokines [N1-F2], which implies that cannabinoid composition and dose matter for cytokine suppression. The synovium review notes that the clinical use of cannabinoids has been reported only in a few studies with small sample sizes and for short periods [N4-F3], which is relevant to time course but not directly about animal studies. Overall, the evidence supports that cannabinoids can be effective in arthritis models, but the provided material is thin on standardized dose-response curves and time-course details across studies [N2-R1][N2-F1][N1-F2].

Safety, tolerability, and limitations of cannabinoid treatments

The provided evidence indicates that cannabinoid treatments are generally well-tolerated in animal studies, but some adverse effects and organ toxicity signals are reported, especially with systemic delivery. A review on toxicity in rhesus monkeys notes elevated liver weights 8–71% and kidney weights 10–155%, plus pulmonary irritation, nephritis, increased BUN, and decreased serum electrolytes, hemoglobin, etc. [N5-R5]. Another review on renal outcomes and other adverse effects of cannabinoids states that the narrative review explores benefits and risks in kidney health, particularly in individuals with pre-existing renal conditions [N5-R2]. A review on liver disease reports that CBD reduced liver inflammation and improved glucose tolerance in mice fed HFD supplemented with CBD, suggesting some safety signals, but also that pre-clinical studies suggest CBD may reduce inflammation and oxidative stress in the liver [N5-R1][N5-R4]. These findings imply that cannabinoids can have organ-specific toxicity, with liver and kidney effects being most clearly documented in the provided evidence.

The evidence also highlights differences between systemic, topical, and localized delivery. The scoping review on cannabis and rheumatoid arthritis states that CBD has an anti-arthritic effect in oral and intraperitoneal administration in CIA, and that preclinical studies have demonstrated promising results in halting disease progression and relieving pain [N2-R1][N2-F1]. This suggests that systemic routes can reach inflammatory sites but may also expose organs to side effects. The topical and transdermal cannabinoid review notes that phytocannabinoids are effective in the treatment of atopic dermatitis, and that topical application of THC reduced certain responses in a rodent study [N6-R1][N6-R5]. The synovium review notes that cannabinoids can be used from a therapeutic perspective to minimize inflammatory and pain processes, and that the endocannabinoid system is present in the inflamed synovium [N4-F3]. Taken together, these sources indicate that topical or localized delivery may reduce systemic exposure and organ toxicity compared to systemic administration, but the provided evidence does not provide a head-to-head comparison of all routes across arthritis studies [N6-R1][N6-R5][N4-F3].

Study limitations and gaps in animal evidence are clear in the provided material. The scoping review explicitly states that there is a scarcity of patient clinical studies, mixed results, and currently no established clinical recommendations [N2-F1]. The synovium review notes that the clinical use of cannabinoids has been reported only in a few studies with small sample sizes and for short periods, and that there are gaps regarding efficacy, dose-dependent curve, tolerability, drug interaction, expected adverse effects, and safety [N4-F3]. A separate review on cannabinoids in rheumatic diseases also mentions that only a limited number of products have been approved for therapy, and that legislation and classification are still non-uniform and inadequate [N4-F3]. These limitations imply that animal evidence is promising but not yet sufficient to support widespread clinical use, and that translational gaps remain in dose-response, tolerability, and long-term safety.

In summary, the evidence suggests that cannabinoids can be effective in arthritis models, but safety and tolerability vary by route and study design. Systemic administration may produce organ toxicity signals in liver and kidney, while topical or localized delivery may reduce systemic exposure [N5-R5][N5-R2][N6-R1][N6-R5]. The animal literature is promising but limited by small sample size, short study periods, mixed results, and insufficient data on dose-response and safety [N2-F1][N4-F3].

Practical treatment implications: dose, route, and study design

Delivery route has a major effect on exposure and whether effects are local or systemic. The provided evidence shows that systemic routes, such as oral or intraperitoneal administration, can reach joint tissues but may also expose organs to side effects [N2-R1][N2-F1]. The topical and transdermal review notes that phytocannabinoids are effective in the treatment of atopic dermatitis, and that topical application of THC reduced certain responses in a rodent study [N6-R1][N6-R5]. The synovium review emphasizes that cannabinoids can be used from a therapeutic perspective to minimize inflammatory and pain processes in rheumatic diseases, and that the endocannabinoid system is present in the inflamed synovium [N4-F3]. This suggests that localized delivery may target the affected joint or synovium more directly, while systemic delivery may act on a broader body, with greater potential for organ toxicity [N6-R1][N6-R5][N4-F3].

The evidence also suggests that route affects local versus systemic effects. Systemic delivery may reduce local inflammation but increase systemic exposure, whereas topical or localized delivery may concentrate effects at the site of disease while minimizing systemic side effects [N6-R1][N6-R5][N4-F3]. The provided search results do not offer a complete comparison of all routes in arthritis models, so this should be treated as a general implication rather than a definitive conclusion. However, the scoping review on cannabis and rheumatoid arthritis states that CBD has an anti-arthritic effect in oral and intraperitoneal administration in CIA, and that preclinical studies have demonstrated promising results in halting disease progression and relieving pain [N2-R1][N2-F1]. This supports the idea that route choice matters for therapeutic potential.

Study design is another key determinant of whether therapeutic potential is captured. The scoping review emphasizes that preclinical studies have demonstrated promising results, but that there is a scarcity of patient clinical studies, mixed results, and no established clinical recommendations [N2-F1]. The synovium review similarly notes that clinical use has been reported only in a few studies with small sample sizes and for short periods, and that gaps remain in efficacy, dose-dependent curve, tolerability, drug interaction, expected adverse effects, and safety [N4-F3]. These limitations suggest that animal models are useful for hypothesis generation and mechanistic insight, but may not fully replicate human disease complexity, especially when sample size, duration, and outcome measures differ from human clinical trials [N2-F1][N4-F3].

Implications for translation from animal models to clinical use are therefore cautious. The evidence supports the potential of cannabinoids in arthritis, but the provided material also highlights major translation barriers: limited clinical data, mixed results, small sample sizes, short study periods, and unclear dose-response and safety profiles [N2-F1][N4-F3]. The safety review further shows that organ toxicity signals exist, especially with systemic delivery, which implies that clinical translation must carefully balance dose, route, and exposure [N5-R5][N5-R2]. Overall, the best study designs for capturing therapeutic potential appear to be those that combine well-controlled animal models with dose-response testing, route comparison, and mechanistic endpoints, while recognizing that these studies do not yet provide a complete basis for clinical recommendation [N2-R1][N2-F1][N4-F3].

## Integrated conclusion on how cannabinoids affect inflammation, pain, and joint changes in chronic inflammatory arthritis

Cannabinoids appear to affect chronic inflammatory arthritis through a combination of anti-inflammatory, pain-relieving, and joint-protective mechanisms, but the evidence base is still largely preclinical and therefore should be interpreted with caution for human translation. Across the branch reports, the consistent picture is that cannabinoids reduce inflammation and pain in arthritis models, may help preserve joint structure, and are generally well-tolerated in animals, although toxicity signals and study limitations remain important caveats.

### 1. Cannabinoids reduce inflammation through CB1/CB2 pathways and cytokine suppression

The biological pathways evidence shows that cannabinoids primarily act through the endocannabinoid system, especially the CB1 and CB2 receptors. A systematic review of in vivo studies states that cannabinoids act on inflammation through mechanisms different from NSAIDs, and that CBD, CBG, and CBD+THC exert a predominantly anti-inflammatory effect in vivo, whereas THC alone does not reduce pro-inflammatory cytokines [N1-F2]. Another review on the CB2 receptor emphasizes that CB2 mediates inflammation in vitro, in animal models, and in the context of clinical trials [N1-R5].

Cannabinoids suppress cytokine production and immune activation by reducing key pro-inflammatory mediators. The same systematic review found that TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, and IFN-γ were consistently reduced after treatment with CBD, CBG, or CBD+THC, while THC alone did not reduce pro-inflammatory cytokine levels [N1-F2]. This indicates that cannabinoids can dampen immune activation and cytokine-driven inflammation in arthritis, which is central to the disease process.

The synovium-focused evidence also supports a broader anti-inflammatory context. The review on cannabinoids in the inflamed synovium states that the endocannabinoid system is present in inflamed synovium and can be a target for rheumatic diseases, with implications for pain, inflammation, and joint metabolism [N4-F3]. This reinforces that cannabinoids can act locally in joint tissue and synovium, not only through cytokine suppression but also through modulation of inflammatory and repair processes [N4-F3].

### 2. Cannabinoids reduce pain, especially mechanical and inflammatory pain

The pain and analgesic mechanisms evidence is similarly consistent. Cannabinoids show consistent evidence of reducing both mechanical and inflammatory pain in animal models of arthritis [N3-R1]. A review on cannabinoids and pain states that cannabinoids may contribute to pain relief through an anti-inflammatory action [N3-R1]. Another review notes that TRPV1 mediates inflammatory pain and that TRPV1/CB1 co-expression is enhanced in inflamed tissue [N3-R2], supporting a receptor-based explanation for analgesia.

CB1 and CB2 are both implicated in pain relief. The broader cannabinoid review reports that interventions targeting CB1 or CB2 receptors improve pain outcomes in a variety of preclinical pain models [N3-R3]. The scoping review on cannabis and rheumatoid arthritis also notes that CBD has an anti-arthritic effect in acute and chronic relapsing collagen-induced arthritis, and that preclinical studies have demonstrated promising results in halting disease progression and relieving pain [N2-R1][N2-F1]. This supports the idea that cannabinoids can relieve pain in arthritis by acting on both inflammatory and nociceptive pathways.

Evidence for central versus peripheral analgesia is thinner than for general pain relief. The strongest direct statement is that TRPV1 mediates inflammatory pain and that TRPV1/CB1 co-expression is increased in inflamed tissue [N3-R2]. The broader evidence suggests a multimodal mechanism rather than a strict separation into central vs peripheral analgesia: cannabinoids appear to reduce pain through anti-inflammatory effects, receptor-mediated suppression of pain signals, and tissue-level healing processes [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N4-F3].

### 3. Cannabinoids affect joint changes and structural outcomes

On joint structural changes, the evidence is more mixed than for inflammation and pain. The animal-model evidence is centered on collagen-induced arthritis (CIA) and related joint disease models. The scoping review reports that oral or intraperitoneal CBD has an anti-arthritic effect in acute and chronic relapsing CIA [N2-R1], and that preclinical studies have demonstrated promising results in halting disease progression and relieving pain [N2-F1]. The synovium review adds that cannabinoids can be used from a therapeutic perspective to minimize inflammatory and pain processes typical of OA and RA, and that the endocannabinoid system is present in the inflamed synovium [N4-F3].

The evidence for cartilage damage, bone erosion, and joint swelling is less uniformly conclusive in the provided material. The branch reports indicate that cannabinoids reduce joint inflammation and pain and may help halt disease progression, but they do not establish that all studies improved cartilage and bone outcomes equally [N2-R1][N2-F1][N4-F3]. The synovium review also notes that the clinical use of cannabinoids has been reported only in a few studies with small sample sizes and for short periods, and that gaps remain in efficacy, dose-dependent curve, tolerability, drug interaction, expected adverse effects, and safety [N4-F3]. So, while there is promising evidence for joint protection, the provided evidence is not sufficient to claim a universal or standardized benefit across all structural endpoints.

### 4. Safety and tolerability: benefit vs risk

The safety evidence suggests that cannabinoids can be well-tolerated in animal studies, but some adverse effects and organ toxicity signals are present. A review on toxicity in rhesus monkeys reports elevated liver weights 8–71% and kidney weights 10–155%, plus pulmonary irritation, nephritis, increased BUN, and decreased serum electrolytes, hemoglobin, etc. [N5-R5]. Another review on renal outcomes and other adverse effects of cannabinoids states that the narrative review explores benefits and risks in kidney health, particularly in individuals with pre-existing renal conditions [N5-R2]. The evidence also highlights differences between systemic, topical, and localized delivery. Systemic routes such as oral or intraperitoneal administration can reach inflammatory sites but may also expose organs to side effects [N2-R1][N2-F1]. Topical and transdermal cannabinoid literature suggests that phytocannabinoids are effective in the treatment of atopic dermatitis and that topical application of THC reduced certain responses in a rodent study [N6-R1][N6-R5]. Taken together, these sources suggest that localized delivery may reduce systemic exposure and organ toxicity compared to systemic administration [N6-R1][N6-R5][N4-F3].

### 5. Dose, route, and study design matter for translation

The practical treatment implications are clear: delivery route strongly affects exposure and whether effects are local or systemic. Systemic administration may reduce local inflammation but increase systemic side effects, while topical or localized delivery may concentrate effects at the site of disease while minimizing systemic toxicity [N2-R1][N2-F1][N6-R1][N6-R5][N4-F3]. The branch reports also emphasize that study design is critical for capturing therapeutic potential.

The animal literature is promising, but limited by small sample sizes, short study periods, mixed results, and insufficient data on dose-response and safety [N2-F1][N4-F3]. The scoping review explicitly states that there is a scarcity of patient clinical studies, mixed results, and currently no established clinical recommendations [N2-F1]. The synovium review similarly notes that clinical use has been reported only in a few studies with small sample sizes and for short periods, and that gaps remain in efficacy, dose-dependent curve, tolerability, drug interaction, expected adverse effects, and safety [N4-F3]. These limitations imply that animal studies are useful for hypothesis generation and mechanistic insight, but they do not yet provide a complete basis for clinical recommendation [N2-F1][N4-F3].

### 6. Overall conclusion

In chronic inflammatory arthritis models, cannabinoids appear to reduce inflammation through CB1/CB2 signaling and cytokine suppression, relieve mechanical and inflammatory pain, and may help preserve joint structure, although the evidence for cartilage and bone outcomes is less uniformly established [N1-F2][N1-R5][N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N4-F3]. The evidence supports a multimodal mechanism in which cannabinoids act centrally, peripherally, and locally in joint tissue, with TRPV1, CB1, and CB2 all playing roles [N3-R2][N3-R3]. However, the provided evidence also shows that systemic cannabinoid exposure can produce organ toxicity, especially in liver and kidney, and that topical or localized delivery may reduce systemic side effects [N5-R5][N5-R2][N6-R1][N6-R5][N4-F3].

For translation from animal models to clinical use, the branch reports point to a cautious optimism: cannabinoids show promise, but the current evidence base is still limited by small sample sizes, short study periods, mixed results, and incomplete safety profiling [N2-F1][N4-F3]. The best study designs for capturing therapeutic potential appear to be those that combine well-controlled animal models with dose-response testing, route comparison, and mechanistic endpoints, while recognizing that these studies do not yet provide a complete basis for clinical recommendation [N2-R1][N2-F1][N4-F3].

In short: cannabinoids affect chronic inflammatory arthritis by reducing inflammation, pain, and possibly joint damage, but the evidence is strongest for anti-inflammatory and analgesic effects, weaker for uniform structural preservation, and cautious about long-term safety and clinical translation [N1-F2][N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N4-F3][N5-R5][N6-R1][N6-R5].

Cannabinoids appear to affect chronic inflammatory arthritis through a combination of anti-inflammatory, pain-relieving, and joint-protective mechanisms, but the evidence base is still largely preclinical and therefore should be interpreted with caution for human translation. Another review on the CB2 receptor emphasizes that CB2 mediates inflammation in vitro, in animal models, and in the context of clinical trials [N1-R5].

Cannabinoids suppress cytokine production and immune activation by reducing key pro-inflammatory mediators. The same systematic review found that TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, and IFN-γ were consistently reduced after treatment with CBD, CBG, or CBD+THC, while THC alone did not reduce pro-inflammatory cytokine levels [N1-F2]. This indicates that cannabinoids can dampen immune activation and cytokine-driven inflammation in arthritis, which is central to the disease process.

The synovium-focused evidence also supports a broader anti-inflammatory context. The review on cannabinoids in the inflamed synovium states that the endocannabinoid system is present in inflamed synovium and can be a target for rheumatic diseases, with implications for pain, inflammation, and joint metabolism [N4-F3]. The broader cannabinoid review reports that interventions targeting CB1 or CB2 receptors improve pain outcomes in a variety of preclinical pain models [N3-R3].
